target_only_tests.note: Eight cases, none counted as ported coverage, in three groups. (1) THREE SEAM-LIVENESS CASES, which D-0014 requires because this file substitutes `sessionRuntime` in exactly three places and every one of those three ported cases asserts a REFUSAL or an ABSENCE -- shapes a substitute that is never reached cannot disturb. `the liveness question is routed through the platform seam` wraps `isPosix` as a pass-through and requires a record-carrying read to consult it, because `test_unknowable_liveness_fails_closed_for_acting_and_open_eyed_for_reading` would pass on Windows whether or not the seam exists. `the durable record is written through the seam, twice, and the second carries the pid` pins BOTH halves of the discriminator the two emergency-kill cases' substitute keys on -- record.json written twice, the first without a pid and the second with one, and `probe-evidence.txt` written through the same member -- because a port that wrote the record once, or wrote the pid first, would leave `refuseTheRecordWriteCarryingAPid` refusing a write that never happens and `test_a_child_whose_pid_cannot_be_recorded_is_not_left_running` asserting that an ordinary start fails. `the stop ladder's first rung is routed through the group seam` pins `[pid, "SIGTERM"]` as the ladder's first act on POSIX and the seam going unreached off it, because `test_a_child_that_outlives_the_emergency_kill_is_not_abandoned` makes `signalGroup` a no-op and would then get its `TIMED_OUT` by accident if production had stopped calling it. Every one of these three patches is a PASS-THROUGH: the real child is still spawned, the real ladder still runs, only the call is recorded. (2) TWO CASES FOR D-0301, the decision that made the five verbs `Promise`-returning. Python's verbs run under one thread and `Popen.poll()` is synchronous, so interlock gets both properties for free and has no case that could lose them; here each is a line of code that can be deleted, and deleting either leaves all 65 ported cases green -- measured, not assumed. `the five verbs are serialised per provider instance` holds `start` inside a pass-through `spawn` and requires `readState` and `listSessions` not to settle across five real macrotask turns, then to settle in FIFO order, because on C2 a lost exclusion lets a read land inside stop()'s TERM -> wait -> SIGKILL -> sweep ladder and lets a second resume bump `record.generation` mid-spawn. `every read of a child's exit status is preceded by a macrotask settle` asserts the member's KIND (a timer armed beforehand has fired when `settleExits()` resolves, where five thousand microtask turns leave it unfired) and then its ROUTING (a settle precedes the first exit-status read and there are at least as many settles as reads), because every other path to an exit status in this file is preceded by an awaited wait or a polling helper that supplies the turn incidentally. (3) THREE ORDERINGS AND ONE DURABLE FIELD the source's own cases observe only by consequence, each added because a mutation proved the property unprotected -- rule 10's failure mode. `a vetoed workspace is neither created nor started`: the ported `test_a_vetoed_workspace_creation_refuses_the_start` asserts a `Failure` whose detail says `vetoed` and nothing else, so it is green whether the veto precedes the directory or follows it and whether or not a child was spawned; creating the workspace above the veto leaves all 65 ported cases green and turns this one red. (The stub's suite pins both halves in its own ported slot; C2's does not, and the ceiling forbids borrowing the stronger assertion into C2's.) `an identity incident is committed to the record, and read back from it`: deleting the persisted-incident branch leaves all 65 green because every ported case that observes an incident can also reach it through the live per-event mismatch scan, and making the incident write skipped leaves `test_an_identity_incident_survives_a_supervisor_restart` green because the second life re-derives the incident from the events file still on disk -- the case named for durability passing with nothing durable. This case deletes the events files and requires the answer to come from the record. `the provider names no control-plane symbol in either spelling` holds the camelCase absence: interlock's package directory and its identifiers are both snake_case, so the source's one `"control_plane"` assertion covers the import and the symbol at once, while continuo's directory is `src/control_plane/` and its identifiers are camelCase (D-0201), making them two different strings. Asserting the second in the ported slot would make that case say more than its source says, so rule 0's ceiling puts it here. Added by a Codex review of the finished belt, each pinning a rule-9 divergence -- a value JavaScript admits that Python's types excluded, so the source's own suite could not construct it and the ported suite could not catch it -- and each demonstrated by breaking the fix again and watching the case go red: `a record whose bytes are not UTF-8 is a broken record, not a mangled one (target-only)`. Python's `read_text(encoding="utf-8")` is strict, so a record carrying a byte that is not legal UTF-8 raises and is answered as a broken record. `readFileSync(path, "utf8")` substitutes U+FFFD instead, so an otherwise well-formed record parsed and could be resumed with a mangled workspace, prompt or argv. No source case can construct this: to interlock a record either decodes or is broken, and there is no third state to assert. D-0015 is the convention this restores. Added by a Codex review of the finished belt, each pinning a rule-9 divergence -- a value JavaScript admits that Python's types excluded, so the source's own suite could not construct it and the ported suite could not catch it -- and each demonstrated by breaking the fix again and watching the case go red: `a record naming pid or pgid 0 is a broken record, not a throw out of a verb (target-only)`. The port is deliberately STRICTER than the source here, and the entry says so rather than claiming parity: CPython's `_optional_int` accepts `0` and `-1` because they are `int's, and interlock survives them only because `os.kill(0, 0)` and `os.killpg(0, sig)` address the caller's own process group. The seam refuses those (it must -- a recorded `0` would aim the stop ladder's SIGKILL at the process running the suite), so without a check at the parse the refusal surfaced as a `RangeError` thrown out of `readState` / `stop` / `resume`, where the contract owes a typed result. The `record.pgid || record.pid` falsy fallback is why a recorded pgid of `0` was the quiet case: it is absorbed into the pid before any seam sees it. Added by a Codex review of the finished belt, each pinning a rule-9 divergence -- a value JavaScript admits that Python's types excluded, so the source's own suite could not construct it and the ported suite could not catch it -- and each demonstrated by breaking the fix again and watching the case go red: `a prompt whose leading whitespace is Python's alone is still refused as a flag (target-only)`. `str.lstrip()` strips per `str.isspace()`; JavaScript's `\s` is a different set, and the guard was wrong in BOTH directions. U+001C is Python whitespace and not `\s`, so `"<U+001C>--resume <uuid>"` was accepted and would have reached the CLI as a flag; U+FEFF is `\s` and not Python whitespace, so `"<U+FEFF>-p is a prompt"` was refused where interlock spawns it. The case pins both directions, because refusing the second would be the port inventing a refusal the source has not got.

approved_non_running.reason: The source's two capability gates -- `@pytest.mark.skipif(not IS_POSIX, ...)` and `@pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_PROC, ...)` -- each bound ONCE, as the factories `posixTest(reason)` and `procTest(reason)`, so the textual construct appears exactly twice for the seven gated cases (2 POSIX + 5 `/proc`) while each case still carries its own reason string verbatim at its call site. Seven spellings of two conditions would be seven approvals for one fact; factoring the reasons out instead would be worse, because the reason is what a CI log prints in place of a result and the source deliberately wrote seven different ones. Re-derived here rather than taken on trust: scripts/parity-check.mjs's NON_RUNNING sweep was re-implemented -- the same five patterns, the same `stripComments` then `blankStrings` pre-pass, the same per-occurrence `match(...g)` count -- and run over this file and over the three files in test/session/helpers/. Result: `skipIf` 2, at lines 180 and 185, and zero for `test.skip`, `test.todo`, `test.fails` and `xfail` in all four files. The two conditions are PROBED, never inferred from `process.platform` (rule 4): `IS_POSIX` is `process.platform !== "win32"`, which is `os.name == "posix"`, and `HAS_PROC` is `statSync("/proc", { throwIfNoEntry: false })?.isDirectory() === true` -- `is_dir()` and not an existence check, because a regular file named `/proc` answers the two predicates differently and the gated cases read `<pid>/cmdline` out of a directory. The platform name would be the wrong question outright: five of the seven reasons are about macOS, which is POSIX and has no `/proc`, so a `platform === "linux"` gate would make those five reasons untrue on the one host they were written for. Both constants are read at module load, which is when pytest evaluates a `skipif` condition.

conditionally_collected.reason: Guarded by the source's `@pytest.mark.skipif(not IS_POSIX, reason="orphan liveness is resolved via POSIX signals")`, carried here as `posixTest("orphan liveness is resolved via POSIX signals")` over a condition probed at module load, as pytest evaluates a `skipif` at collection time. pytest COLLECTS a skipped test and `vitest list` OMITS one, so on a Windows host this id is absent from the collection while the case is still declared, still mapped, and still runs on every POSIX host. It ran on the porting host and runs on this repository's Ubuntu cells. The checker still requires the title to be present in the file's source text, and it is -- `"test_an_orphans_record_is_detected_by_the_next_supervisor_life"` is the quoted first argument at test/session/claude-cli-provider.test.ts line 928 -- so a deletion or a rename fails here rather than being excused.

Absent from `vitest list` on a host with no `/proc` -- macOS is the host the reason was written for, and it is POSIX, so the platform name does not answer this question. This is the case that pins the reclaim ORDER issue #17 fixes (resolve the survivor before considering `--resume`, so no second live writer is minted), which is why it is named explicitly rather than covered by a pattern. notes: Target ids are the source function names verbatim, `parametrize` expansions included, and no case sits inside a `describe` -- the same convention as this belt's first ledger, and for the same reason: with the id a lookup rather than a judgement, this ledger's mapping cannot disagree with the file. The eleven expansions carry pytest's own ids through test/testkit/parametrize.ts in the source's `ids=[...]` order (`bare-string-args`, `nul-in-args`, `empty-prompt`, `non-string-prompt`, `blank-resume`, `flag-shaped-prompt`; then `session-id`, `resume-eq`, `print`, `continue`, `resume-attached`). Reconciled in both directions at the end of this ledger's own verification: the 65 inventory node ids and the 65 `test_`-prefixed target ids `vitest list --json` collects are equal AS SEQUENCES, not merely as sets, and the 8 remaining collected ids are exactly the declared target-only ones. 65 + 8 = 73, which is what `npx vitest run test/session/claude-cli-provider.test.ts` reports passing.

63 ported and 2 adapted, re-derived against the source rather than taken from the file header. The two adapted cases are the only two in the file that read a Python `__doc__` (`ClaudeCliSessionProvider._start_session.__doc__` and `ClaudeCliSessionProvider.resume.__doc__`), and each is marked `ADAPTED.` at its head in the target so the count is auditable from the code. Everything else that could have been adapted was checked and was not: `test_the_provider_imports_nothing_from_the_control_plane` is `ported`, because its ONE source assertion (`"control_plane" not in S2_SOURCE`) is carried unchanged -- the camelCase absence continuo additionally needs is a target-only case at the end of the file, not a second line in the ported slot, because rule 0's ceiling makes asserting more as wrong as asserting less. The two module-text reads that both adapted cases and that import lint depend on go through `repoSource`, which refuses a `dist/` path: `tsc` strips comments, so a build artefact would make the presence assertions fail loudly and the absence assertion pass unconditionally.

What is real here and what is substituted, because it bears on how much these 65 rows are worth. The normal path drives a REAL child process -- a small stand-in for the `claude` executable, rendering only the public surface the source's probes recorded -- so the grandchild sweep, the process-group signalling and the spawn-error classification are proved against the operating system rather than against a mock. `sessionRuntime` is substituted in exactly three places, each a branch no real child can reach: `isPosix` (the Windows-equivalent liveness refusal), `writeAtomic` (a record write that fails with ENOSPC) and `signalGroup` (a signal delivered nowhere, so the child genuinely survives its own SIGKILL). Those three correspond to the source's three `monkeypatch.setattr` sites. Every OTHER `patchSeam` call in the file is a pass-through belonging to a target-only liveness case: it records that a member was called and delegates to the real one. Two target-side details are not the source's and nothing observes them: every deliberately hanging child is given a 30-second bounded sleep instead of the fake's 60 (so a missed kill self-heals inside the run rather than holding an `events-NNN.jsonl` open on the Windows cell), and the teardown WAITS for the exits it asks for, which the source's fixture does not need to.

The `conditionally_collected` escape hatch was checked in both directions on this file, as rule 4 asks. With the capability present -- this host is POSIX and has `/proc`, so all seven gated ids are collected -- the check passes and the declarations are simply unused. The absent-host path is the one that matters and it is exercised by construction: `absentButDeclared` only returns true after `declaresTitle` finds the quoted title in the file, so a gated case that was deleted or renamed away still reports `missing` rather than being excused, and each of the seven titles was confirmed present as a quoted string literal at the line named in its row. No wildcards: the seven ids are written out.

entries.reason: One assertion is re-pointed at a member interlock does not have. The source asserts `result.kind is FailureKind.UNINTERPRETABLE_RESPONSE`, which in interlock is the only kind an identity incident can carry: its `FailureKind` has six members and none of them is identity-specific. continuo #92 measured what that costs at the layer above -- the orchestrator could not tell an impounded identity from a child that wrote a line of garbage, so the refusal class its caller saw depended on which of two detection paths won a race against the child. continuo D-0047 adds `FailureKind.IDENTITY_INCIDENT` and this case now asserts that. The other two assertions are unchanged -- `"identity incident" in detail` and `provider_detail["expected"]` -- and the substituted one is neither weaker nor stronger: both spellings pin exactly one member of a closed vocabulary, and the fact under test (a disagreeing identity is an incident, reported as a typed failure with the committed id attached) is the source cases own. This is a deliberate divergence under D-0023, recorded in `divergences` below; nothing here is a translation difficulty.

One of the three assertions has no runtime form in TypeScript. The first two are unchanged -- `"never relied on as a lock" in S2_SOURCE` and `"U27" in S2_SOURCE` -- over the same whole module text, read here by `repoSource("src/session/claude_cli_provider.ts")`. The third reads `ClaudeCliSessionProvider._start_session.__doc__`, a string the interpreter binds onto the function; a JSDoc block is a comment and is gone before anything runs, so it is re-pointed at this module's own source text as `docBlockBefore(S2_SOURCE, methodDeclaration("_startSession"))` and the substring checked is the source's, character for character. It must be the `.ts` and never `dist/`: `tsc` strips comments, so a build artefact would fail the two presence assertions visibly and satisfy every absence assertion unconditionally (rule 10) -- `repoSource` refuses a `dist/` path for that reason. The property is at least as strongly pinned. `docBlockBefore` is bounded to ONE block and requires that only whitespace separate it from the declaration, so it cannot be satisfied by a file-wide hit (which the first assertion already covers) nor by the neighbouring block, which belongs to `resume` and is the block the other adapted case in this file reads. Python's `__doc__` needs no such guard because the interpreter does the binding; the port has to check what the interpreter would have guaranteed.

Both assertions read `ClaudeCliSessionProvider.resume.__doc__`, and for the same reason as above there is nothing to read at runtime. Both are re-pointed at `docBlockBefore(S2_SOURCE, methodDeclaration("resume"))` and the two substrings -- `"U32"` then `"lease"` -- are the source's, in the source's order. This case is the one that makes the adjacency requirement load-bearing rather than decorative: `_startSession`'s block is `resume`'s neighbour in `src/session/claude_cli_provider.ts`, so a file-wide or nearest-preceding-block search would let one method's documentation answer for the other's, and the two blocks' recorded sentences differ. Bounded and adjacency-checked, the port asserts strictly more than a text search would and exactly what `__doc__` gives Python for free.

inherited_limitations.what: `test_stop_of_a_record_whose_pid_is_now_a_stranger_touches_nothing` makes three claims in its name and its comment -- the stop signals nothing, sweeps nothing unverified, and reports the session as itself -- and asserts only the third. Its two assertions are `Ok` and `observation === COULD_NOT_OBSERVE`; nothing records what was signalled or swept, so a stop that DID signal the recorded pid would satisfy both. What stands in for the missing assertion is incidental rather than designed: the planted pid is the test runner's own, so a stop that signalled it would kill the run -- which surfaces as a crashed worker, not as this case going red, and which would be defeated by any signal that is not fatal by default or by a handler installed in the runner. Reproduced exactly, not improved.
inherited_limitations.source: tests/session/test_claude_cli_provider.py::test_stop_of_a_record_whose_pid_is_now_a_stranger_touches_nothing -- `_plant_record(..., pid=os.getpid(), pgid=os.getpid())`, then `assert isinstance(result, Ok)` and `assert result.value.observation is Observation.COULD_NOT_OBSERVE`. Both transcribed unchanged; the docstring's other two claims are carried into the port as a comment, exactly as unasserted there as here.
inherited_limitations.where_a_fix_belongs: Here. interlock is frozen (D-0023), so the ported slot's missing assertion is closed on this side or not at all, and the port already has the seam it would need: `sessionRuntime.signalGroup` wrapped as a pass-through is how the three target-only liveness cases in this file are written, and the same shape would let a case require the signal list to be empty. It was not added in the pass that wrote this entry, because rule 0's ceiling forbids strengthening the ported slot and a new target-only case was outside this file's agreed scope; the gap is disclosed here rather than closed quietly, so the ledger does not report coverage the suite does not have. The belt that next opens this file adds the target-only case.

inherited_limitations.what: For a child that exits by signal, the readout's `provider_state` renders as `exited-<returncode>` with Python's SIGNED convention -- a SIGTERM'd child is the string `exited--15`, with two hyphens -- and no case on either side observes the digits. `test_stop_terminates_a_running_child_and_reports_what_is_left` asserts `startsWith("exited-")` and stops there; `test_stop_of_an_already_exited_child_is_a_readout_not_an_error` compares against the child's own word `completed`; the only exact `returncode` any case in this file pins is `0`. So the part of the string that supervisor code actually parses past the prefix is unpinned. THE PORT'S WINDOW IS WIDER THAN THE SOURCE'S, and that is worth saying plainly: Node reports a child's death as an `(exitCode, signalCode)` pair and never produces Python's negative number, so `toPythonReturncode` in src/session/runtime.ts has to SYNTHESISE it by looking the signal name up in `os.constants.signals` and negating -- a mapping CPython performs itself and that no case in this belt exercises. A wrong sign, or a wrong table lookup, would be green today.
inherited_limitations.source: src/claude_org_runtime/session/claude_cli_provider.py line 1488, `provider_state=f"exited-{returncode}"`, transcribed as `providerState: `exited-${String(returncode)}`` in src/session/claude_cli_provider.ts; and tests/session/test_claude_cli_provider.py line 546, `assert readout.provider_state.startswith("exited-")`, the only assertion the source makes about a signalled child's word. The `-N` convention itself is `subprocess.Popen.returncode`'s, and the port reproduces it deliberately rather than substituting Node's spelling -- the double hyphen included -- because other ported cases compare the whole string.
inherited_limitations.where_a_fix_belongs: Both sides, and the two halves belong in different places. The unobserved digits are interlock's gap: a case that kills a child with a known signal and asserts the exact `exited--15` would close it, and should be written there first, because a target-only case pinning a rendering interlock's own suite leaves open would make the two suites disagree about what the string is allowed to be. The synthesis is the PORT's own and is a fair subject for a target-side case as soon as `src/session/runtime.ts` acquires a test file of its own; today it has none, which is why this is recorded here rather than fixed.

inherited_limitations.what: Where `/proc` does not exist -- macOS, or a hardened mount -- the post-exit group sweep does nothing at all: `groupMemberCarriesMarker` returns `false` without looking, so no group is signalled and a TERM-ignoring grandchild of an already-exited leader survives the stop. The two cases that would catch it are skipped on exactly those hosts by the same condition, so the platform where the behaviour is weakest is the platform where it is untested. The port reproduces the fallback and its reasoning verbatim rather than inventing a macOS roster.
inherited_limitations.source: `_group_member_carries_marker` in src/claude_org_runtime/session/claude_cli_provider.py: `proc = Path("/proc"); if not proc.is_dir(): return False`, with the docstring's reason carried into `SessionRuntime.groupMemberCarriesMarker` in src/session/runtime.ts. The source states the consequence in its own words, in the skipif reason on `test_stop_reaps_a_group_member_that_outlived_the_leader`: 'where /proc does not exist (macOS) the sweep deliberately does nothing rather than signal an unverifiable group, so a TERM-ignoring survivor of an exited leader is a documented platform limitation, not a behaviour to assert'.
inherited_limitations.where_a_fix_belongs: Nowhere available, and NOT by widening the fallback. The alternative the source rejected is signalling a group whose membership cannot be proven to be this session's, which on a recycled pgid kills a stranger: killing what cannot be proven ours is the worse failure, and both sides keep that choice. A real fix means a macOS-specific roster (`libproc` / `sysctl`) that interlock does not have and that no case on either side would exercise, so building one here would put a security-relevant divergence in the port and leave it untested on the only host it targets. The platform limitation stands as disclosed.

divergences.what: An identity incident is reported as `FailureKind.IDENTITY_INCIDENT`, where interlock reports `FailureKind.UNINTERPRETABLE_RESPONSE`.
divergences.source_behaviour: interlock's `FailureKind` is a six-member closed vocabulary with no identity-specific member, so `claude_cli_provider.py` reports every identity incident as `UNINTERPRETABLE_RESPONSE` -- the same kind it uses for a line that is not JSON, a `result` event naming no outcome, and a capture file it cannot read.
divergences.detail: continuo adds a seventh member and emits it from the two places an identity incident is built (`#readout's persisted-incident branch and its live mismatch scan) plus `resume's own record-incident guard; every verb that converts an uninterpretable readout into a `Failure` now forwards the kind the readout carries instead of hard-coding one. Sites that are NOT identity incidents keep `UNINTERPRETABLE_RESPONSE`, including the two `finished without any event naming a session identity` branches -- those are `never read back`, not `positively contradicted`, and their ported cases (`test_a_finished_child_that_never_named_its_identity_is_not_accepted`) are untouched.
divergences.why: Without a typed discriminator the orchestrator has only two ways to recognise an identity incident: split on `UNINTERPRETABLE_RESPONSE` (which misclassifies broken output as an identity conflict) or match on the `detail` prose (which makes a message an internal protocol). Both were rejected in continuo#92s independent review before this was taken.
divergences.parity_cost: One ported assertion in this file moves (the entry above, now `adapted`), and one target-only assertion in the file `parity/session.provider-contract.ledger.json` covers moves with it (`FailureKind.members.length` 6 -> 7).
